title: How a large language model like Opus 5.5 works
goal: Understand how a large language model turns a prompt into an answer: tokens, the context window, the transformer layers, next-token prediction, the loop that builds the answer, and how training shaped the model.

includes: How large language models of this kind work in general, from a prompt to an answer
What Anthropic publishes about Claude Opus 5.5, such as the context window and the tool use loop
excludes: Anthropic does not publish the architecture, size, or training data of Opus 5.5. This board explains how models like it work in general, not the details of Opus 5.5
Safety training, image input, and the speed tricks that serving systems use

groups.label: Your prompt goes in
groups.description: Turning your text into tokens and holding them in the window.

groups.label: Inside the transformer
groups.description: The layers that turn those tokens into a prediction. A real model repeats them many times.

groups.label: Writing the answer
groups.description: Picking one token at a time, and reaching outside the model.

groups.label: Outside the model
groups.description: The app and tools that act on what the model writes.

groups.label: How it was made
groups.description: The two training stages before you ever send a prompt.

components.label: Tokenizer
components.summary: Cuts your text into tokens, short pieces of words, and numbers each one.
components.explanation:
A model never reads letters. It reads **tokens**. A common word is often one token, and a rare word may be several.

The size of the window is counted in tokens. For Opus 5.5, Anthropic says 1M tokens is roughly 555k words.

references.label: Claude Opus 5.5 overview
references.path: Claude API docs: Models, Claude Opus 5.5
references.note: Documented: 1M tokens is roughly 555k words. The tokenizer description is this board's explanation.

components.label: Context window
components.summary: The model's working memory: your prompt, the chat so far, and the answer so far.
components.explanation:
The window holds everything the model can use for the next token, including the answer it is writing. It is **not** the training data. The model does not look anything up in that.

Opus 5.5 has a 1M-token window. When a conversation grows past what fits, an app has to shorten it, for example by summarizing the older parts.

references.label: Context windows
references.note: Everything in the request counts, including the output.

components.label: Embeddings
components.summary: Turns each token number into a vector, a list of numbers that can be compared.
components.explanation: The vector for a token starts out the same wherever the token appears, and learning during training put similar words near each other. The model also adds information about each token's **position**, because order matters.

components.label: Attention
components.summary: Lets each token look at earlier tokens and weigh which ones matter.
components.explanation:
In the sentence "The dog chased the cat because it was fast", attention helps decide what "it" refers to. Each token mixes in information from the tokens that score as relevant.

A model usually runs many attention "heads" side by side, and each head can focus on a different kind of link.
inputs: Vectors for all tokens so far
outputs: Vectors that carry context from other tokens

components.label: Feed-forward layers
components.summary: Transforms each token's vector on its own. The pair then repeats in the next layer.
components.explanation:
A transformer stacks the same pair many times: attention, then feed-forward. Each pass refines the vectors. Early layers tend to capture simple patterns, and later layers more abstract ones.

Much of what the model knows is stored in the numbers (weights) of these layers, but nobody can point to one fact in one place.
outputs: Refined vectors, passed to the next layer

components.label: Next-token prediction
components.summary: Gives every possible next token a score: how likely is it to come next?
components.explanation: The model does exactly one job: given the tokens so far, rate every possible next token. Writing an essay, a function, or an answer is that one job, repeated.
inputs: The final vector of the last token
outputs: A probability for every possible next token

components.label: Sampling
components.summary: Picks one token from those scores. Temperature sets how random the pick is.
components.explanation: A setting called temperature makes the pick more or less random. Always taking the top token gives the same text every time. Sampling takes a likely token, sometimes not the top one, so the same prompt can give different answers.

components.label: Generation loop
components.summary: Adds the chosen token to the context and runs the pass again, until a stop token.
components.explanation:
The loop adds the token to the context window and runs the whole pass again, until the model writes a stop token. The answer is written **one token at a time**. After each token the model reads the longer context again. Production systems reuse work from earlier passes so that this is fast, but the idea stays the same.

The loop also stops when the output limit is reached. Opus 5.5 can write up to 128K tokens in one answer.

references.label: Context windows
references.note: Documented: each response becomes part of the next input.

references.label: Claude Opus 5.5 overview
references.path: Claude API docs: Models, Claude Opus 5.5
references.note: Documented: up to 128K output tokens. The loop mechanism is this board's explanation.

components.label: Tool use
components.summary: The model writes a tool call, the app runs it, and the result joins the context.
components.explanation:
Tool use is ordinary text generation that follows a format. The model does not run anything. It stops with a request such as "call this tool with these arguments".

For tools that you define, your application runs the call and sends back the result. The model then continues with that result in its context.
inputs: A tool call written by the model
outputs: A tool result for the context window

references.label: Tool use with Claude
references.path: Claude API docs: Tool use overview
references.note: A tool_use block, then a tool_result block.

components.label: Pretraining
components.summary: The model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token.
components.explanation:
At first the model's numbers are random. The training run shows it text, checks its guesses against the real next token, and nudges a very large number of weights to guess better. Then it repeats this at enormous scale.

This stage builds most of what the model knows. It learns language, facts, and patterns of reasoning. It does not yet follow instructions well.
inputs: A very large body of text
outputs: A model that continues text well

components.label: Fine-tuning with feedback
components.summary: Feedback from people and AI teaches it to follow instructions and be helpful.
components.explanation:
People and AI models compare answers and say which is better. Training then pushes the model toward the preferred kind of answer. Anthropic has described methods such as learning from human feedback and Constitutional AI, where an AI model applies written principles.

The weights that come out of this stage are the numbers that every layer uses when you send a prompt.
inputs: Feedback on which answers are better
outputs: The weights used when you send a prompt

relationships.label: the chosen token
relationships.explanation: The loop adds this token to the context window, then runs the layers again.

relationships.label: a tool call, then a pause
relationships.explanation: The model stops after it writes a tool call. The loop continues when the result arrives.

items.text: This board assumes Opus 5.5 follows the broad recipe of today's large language models: a transformer that predicts the next token, trained in two stages.
Anthropic does not publish the architecture of Opus 5.5: the number of layers, the size of the vectors, the kind of attention, or whether it uses experts.
Anthropic does not publish how many parameters (weights) Opus 5.5 has.
The mix of training data is not published. The docs list only cutoff dates (June 2026).
The exact mix of human and AI feedback, and the steps in the recipe, are not published for Opus 5.5.
The vocabulary and the method of the tokenizer are not described. Anthropic says only how many words a million tokens hold.
Opus 5.5 always uses adaptive thinking and decides how much to think before it answers. How does it make that choice inside the loop?

scenarios.title: From a prompt to the first token
scenarios.summary: One pass through the model for the prompt "The capital of France is".

steps.caption: The tokenizer cuts the prompt into tokens and gives each one a number.
The tokens sit in the context window, together with any earlier conversation.
Each token becomes a vector, and the model adds where it sits in the sentence.
Attention lets "is" look back at "capital" and "France". The feed-forward layers then refine each vector. A real model repeats this pair many times.
The last vector becomes a score for every token. "Paris" gets a very high one.
Sampling picks a token, most likely "Paris".

scenarios.title: One token at a time
scenarios.summary: How a whole answer grows out of a single prediction step.

steps.caption: The chosen token goes to the generation loop.
The loop appends the token to the context window. The answer so far is now part of the input.
The loop runs the layers again with the longer context, and predicts the next token.
This repeats until the model writes a stop token or reaches the output limit.

scenarios.title: How the model learned
scenarios.summary: The two training stages that happen before your prompt. The details for Opus 5.5 are not public.

steps.caption: Pretraining: the model reads a very large body of text and practices predicting the next token.
Fine-tuning: feedback from people and AI models teaches it to follow instructions and to give helpful, honest answers.
The final weights are what the layers use for every prompt you send.

scenarios.title: Using a tool
scenarios.summary: How a model that only writes text can still act.

steps.caption: While writing, the model produces a structured tool call, for example a request for the weather.
The model stops. The application runs the tool, because the model cannot.
The application sends the result back. It goes into the context window like any other text.
The generation loop continues, and the model writes its answer using the result.
